claim: Claude Code's permission rules and sandbox cover Claude's tool calls, while plugin command hooks and monitors run with full user permissions and those components, stdio MCP and LSP server processes, and mod-started processes run outside the sandbox.
why: Claude's calls to plugin MCP tools and its Bash commands that run plugin executables are still subject to permission rules.
check: Review the hooks, monitors, stdio MCP servers, LSP servers and mod-started processes of enabled plugins for code you are relying on the sandbox or tool permission rules to contain.
quote: command hooks and monitors are shell commands that run with your full user permissions. Claude Code runs hooks, monitors, MCP servers, LSP servers, and the processes a [mod](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview.md#what-a-mod-can-reach) starts outside the sandbox.

claim: When auto-update is on for a plugin's marketplace, Claude Code updates the plugin in the background, so code reviewed at install time (hooks, bin/, MCP commands) can change on disk later.
why: An update can replace reviewed files with a new version, so review of the installed copy covers only that version.
check: For a plugin with hooks or executables, check whether marketplace auto-update can replace the reviewed version and whether that matches the setup's update policy.
quote: Claude Code updates that plugin in the background, so the files you reviewed can change on disk.

claim: Installing a plugin also enables it, unless its manifest or marketplace entry sets defaultEnabled: false and the user has not enabled it.
why: An install can enable executable components without a separate enable step.
check: Check which installed plugins are enabled and review their hooks, monitors and servers, taking account of plugins whose default is disabled.
quote: Installing a plugin also enables it, unless its manifest or marketplace entry sets [`defaultEnabled: false`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/install#choose-an-install-scope) and you haven't enabled it yourself.

claim: The /plugin Will install summary shows that a hook exists without showing what it runs, while claude plugin details <name> prints a Component inventory for the installed copy, including each hook's event.
why: The Will install summary shows that a hook exists but not its command, so a review has to read the files.
check: When auditing a plugin, read hooks/hooks.json, .mcp.json and every file in bin/ rather than relying on the install summary.
quote: The **Will install** section shows that a hook exists but not what it runs, so read these files in the plugin's directory:

claim: Through managed settings an administrator can limit hooks to those from managed settings and force-enabled plugins, turn off --plugin-dir, --plugin-url and CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, and stop claude.ai-account plugins from loading via syncClaudeAiPlugins.
why: Managed settings let an administrator enforce these controls across the organization, with the scope of each key described in the control matrix.
check: If the organization requires restrictions on hooks, sideloading or account-synced plugins, verify the corresponding managed controls are set.
quote:
* Turn off the `--plugin-dir` and `--plugin-url` flags and the `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` variable
* Limit hooks to those from managed settings and force-enabled plugins
* Stop plugins from members' claude.ai accounts from loading in Claude Code, with [`syncClaudeAiPlugins`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/org#control-matrix)

claim: A marketplace using an official or community name whose source is outside github.com/anthropics/ is refused at load, and the plugins installed from it stop loading; archive sources pinned with sha256 fail the install on a digest mismatch.
why: Claude Code reserves official and community marketplace names for Anthropic's GitHub repositories and verifies archive integrity separately when an entry pins a digest.
check: For official or community marketplace names, use claude plugin marketplace list to verify the source is under github.com/anthropics/, and check for an integrity error if a pinned archive fails to install.
quote: when a marketplace uses an official or community name but its source is outside `github.com/anthropics/

claim: Uninstalling a plugin leaves its files under ~/.claude/plugins/cache/ for 14 days, and orphaned directories stay after the last plugin is uninstalled until another install; the persistent data directory is deleted by default when the last scope is removed.
why: Removal of a distrusted plugin is not immediate on disk.
check: After removing a plugin that was distrusted, check ~/.claude/plugins/cache/<marketplace>/<plugin>/ and delete it by hand if the code must not remain.
quote: the plugin's files stay on disk under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/` for 14 days before a

claim: By default, auto mode trusts only the working directory and the current repository's configured remotes and blocks actions such as pushing to the company's source-control organization or writing to a team bucket unless that destination is added to autoMode.environment.
why: The classifier uses the environment to distinguish trusted destinations from potential exfiltration targets.
check: If an auto-mode setup keeps hitting blocks on its own org's repos, buckets or domains, look for missing autoMode.environment entries in ~/.claude/settings.json or managed settings.
quote: By default, the classifier trusts only the working directory and the current repo's configured remotes.

claim: By default in auto mode Claude can push to the current repository, including its default branch, without a prompt and open a pull request there when the task asks for one, and permissions.ask can add a human checkpoint.
why: Some pushes and pull requests are blocked by default, such as a push with a secret or a pull request to another repository.
check: If a team expects human review before pushes or pull requests in auto mode, verify that its permission rules or PreToolUse hook cover the relevant commands.
quote: By default in auto mode, Claude can push to the repository you're working in, including its default branch, without a prompt. It can also open pull requests there when your task asks for one.

claim: A permissions.ask rule such as Bash(git push *) does not match git -C <dir> push or git -c <key>=<value> push, and a PreToolUse hook is the documented option for a checkpoint that inspects the full command text.
why: The example Bash rules only match commands that begin with the specified prefix.
check: If an audit requires a human checkpoint across command forms, check whether the ask rules cover the commands in use or a PreToolUse hook inspects the full command text.
quote: A push Claude writes another way, such as `git -C <dir> push` or `git -c <key>=<value> push`, [doesn't match the rule](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#bash-rule-limits), so it isn't checkpointed. For a checkpoint that inspects the full command text, add a [PreToolUse hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#pretooluse).

claim: In auto mode, a matching content-scoped `permissions.ask` rule is evaluated before the classifier, prompts for human approval by default, and prevents classifier auto-approval, while `permissions.deny` blocks before the classifier with no override by the classifier or user intent, and a one-off boundary stated in conversation can be lost at compaction.
why: The permission system runs first and the classifier is only a second gate.
check: For a required human checkpoint in auto mode, check that a content-scoped `permissions.ask` rule matches the commands that need approval, and for an action that must never run, look for a matching `permissions.deny` rule.
quote: Blocks before the classifier is consulted. Neither the classifier nor user intent can override it.

claim: The classifier reads the same CLAUDE.md content Claude loads, so a line such as never force push steers both Claude and the classifier.
why: The docs name CLAUDE.md as the first place for project conventions and behavioral rules; autoMode is for rules that cross projects.
check: Check that project conventions about destructive actions are in CLAUDE.md rather than duplicated in a per-project autoMode block, which the classifier ignores.
quote: so an instruction like "never force push" in your project's CLAUDE.md steers both Claude and the classifier at the same time.

claim: autoMode entries from user, managed and --settings or Agent SDK scopes are combined additively, so a developer-added allow entry can override an organization soft_deny entry, and managed permissions.deny blocks matching calls before the classifier runs.
why: Allow rules act as exceptions to soft block rules inside the classifier.
check: For an organization-wide prohibition that must block matching tool calls before classification, verify it is in managed permissions.deny.
quote: a developer-added `allow` entry can override an organization `soft_deny` entry: the combination is additive, not a hard policy boundary.

claim: Classifier precedence in auto mode is hard_deny first (unconditional), then soft_deny, with allow entries and explicit user intent able to override only soft_deny; a general request like clean up the repo is not explicit intent to force-push.
why: hard_deny is for actions to block even when the user asks; soft_deny is for destructive actions that intent can clear.
check: Rules that must hold even when the user asks go in hard_deny or permissions.deny; a soft_deny entry for such a rule is a finding.
quote: `hard_deny` rules block unconditionally. User intent and `allow` exceptions don't apply.

claim: In auto mode, narrow Bash and PowerShell allow rules apply before the classifier by default, unless the command carries per-command allowed domains.
why: A narrow rule can let an unexpected destructive argument through without classifier review.
check: Review narrow shell rules in permissions.allow, especially script and interpreter prefixes, and check whether the commands use per-command allowed domains, since auto mode already drops broad rules such as Bash(*).
quote: By default, narrow Bash and PowerShell allow rules such as `Bash(npm test)` stay in effect. Claude Code resolves them before the classifier runs, unless the command carries [per-command allowed domains](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#per-command-allowed-domains-in-auto-mode).

claim: In classifier requests sent by Claude Code, the classifier reads user messages and commands but not their output, so a user's message stating a repository is public can reach it while the gh repo view output alone cannot.
why: The classifier needs readable evidence of visibility when the repository's remote host and name do not already indicate it.
check: If repository visibility matters to auto mode, check whether it is indicated by the remote, set in autoMode.environment or stated by the user, since the output of a visibility check alone does not reach the classifier.
quote: the classifier reads your messages and the commands Claude runs, not their output.

claim: By default a host or namespace counts as a sensitive remote target when prod or production is a whole word in its name, so prod-db counts and webprod01 does not, and protected namespaces or sensitive targets can be named in autoMode.environment.
why: Protected deployment namespaces fall back to the Sensitive remote targets default until you name them.
check: Compare production hosts and namespaces with the whole-word prod or production default and check whether targets outside it are named in autoMode.environment.
quote: By default, a host or namespace counts as a sensitive remote target when `prod` or `production` is a whole word in its name. For example, `prod-db` counts and `webprod01` doesn't.

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.257, the auto mode classifier blocks requests for the host's own credentials until Host containment in autoMode.environment names the identity the task uses.
why: The default assumes an ordinary developer machine or CI runner with open internet.
check: For containers, VMs or pods with restricted egress or neighbors Claude must avoid, check the version and whether Host containment names allowed hosts, metadata access and the cloud project, cluster or registry and its identity.
quote: Until this entry names that identity, the classifier [blocks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#what-the-classifier-blocks-by-default) requests for the host's own credentials. Requires Claude Code v2.1.257 or later

claim: Setting autoMode.environment alone leaves the default allow, soft_deny and hard_deny lists intact, and /auto-mode-setup drafts entries from the project and recent sessions and writes them to ~/.claude/settings.json if you accept the draft.
why: Only lists that are set are replaced, and only when they omit "$defaults".
check: Check each list in autoMode for "$defaults"; an allow, soft_deny or hard_deny list without it drops all built-in rules for that list.
quote: Run `/auto-mode-setup` to have Claude Code draft `autoMode.environment` entries, and sometimes [rule entries](#override-the-block-and-allow-rules) too, from your project and your recent sessions in it. If you accept the draft, Claude Code writes it to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

claim: The claude auto-mode subcommands expose local rule data, and the server's built-in rules can differ even when /status shows Auto mode server as Enabled.
why: No claude auto-mode subcommand prints the server's built-in rules.
check: Use config for the four effective local lists, defaults for the local built-ins, defaults --label to filter them, critique to flag problematic custom rules and reset to remove autoMode from user settings only, while treating Auto mode server in /status solely as an indicator of server use.
quote: the server's built-in rules can differ from this output, and no `claude auto-mode` subcommand prints them.

claim: A PermissionDenied hook receives the exact input of auto mode denials as tool_input, whereas the Recently blocked tab approval only lets Claude retry and adds no permission rule, so the retried action can be blocked again.
why: Repeated denials can call for an environment entry for a needed destination, an allow rule for a standing exception, or stated intent for a one-off action.
check: For repeated auto mode denials, inspect which action or destination was blocked before changing rules, and check for a PermissionDenied hook if programmatic logging is needed.
quote: Approving an action doesn't add a permission rule. In auto mode, a retried action goes through the check again, so it can be blocked again.

claim: In the auto mode transcript, Not run · auto mode's check had no usable answer or Auto mode could not evaluate this action means Claude Code blocked the call without a classifier verdict, while Blocked by auto mode means the classifier judged it unsafe.
why: A missing verdict calls for classifier troubleshooting, while an unsafe verdict can call for an environment entry, an allow rule or stated intent depending on the action.
check: When a user reports auto mode denials, separate no-verdict errors from classifier blocks before adding autoMode entries.
quote: A dim `Not run · auto mode's check had no usable answer` row, or text that reports a problem with the classifier itself, such as `Auto mode could not evaluate this action`, means Claude Code blocked the call without a verdict from the classifier.

claim: Anthropic reports that users accept 93% of manual permission prompts and presents auto mode as a middle ground between manual review and running without permission guardrails.
why: Repeated approval prompts can lead to approval fatigue, where people stop paying close attention to what they approve.
check: When a workflow relies on manual prompts for high-stakes review, check whether reviewers have the time and context to examine the actions they approve.
quote: Manual prompts sit in the middle, and in practice users accept 93% of them anyway.

claim: Anthropic measured a 17% false-negative rate for the full auto mode pipeline on 52 curated real overeager actions.
why: In most misses Anthropic examined, the classifier spotted the danger but misjudged whether the consent in the session covered the specific action.
check: Check whether the setup assumes auto mode reliably catches actions that exceed the user's consent.
quote: The 17% false-negative rate on real overeager actions is the honest number. The agent was trying to solve the user's problem and tried to execute a dangerous command past what was authorized.

claim: In auto mode, in-project file writes and edits skip the classifier, which reviews calls that reach the final tier, including shell commands, web fetches, external tool calls, subagent spawns and filesystem operations outside the project.
why: In-project edits are reviewable through version control and would otherwise add classifier latency.
check: For a setup expecting auto mode to review in-project writes or edits, verify that any required review is supplied by another control.
quote: File writes and edits inside the project directory are allowed without a classifier call.

claim: On entering auto mode Claude Code drops allow rules known to grant arbitrary code execution, including blanket shell access, wildcarded script interpreters such as python, node and ruby, and package-manager run commands, while narrow rules carry over; the list is best-effort and incomplete.
why: Leaving those rules active would mean the classifier never sees the commands most capable of damage.
check: Audit permissions.allow for interpreter or package-manager wildcards that auto mode may not catch, since any list is incomplete.
quote: we drop permission rules that are known to grant arbitrary code execution, including blanket shell access, wildcarded script interpreters (python, node, ruby, and similar), and package manager run commands. While this is best-effort based on real-world usage, any list will inevitably be incomplete.

claim: In the auto mode pipeline Anthropic describes, the transcript classifier receives user messages and bare tool calls with assistant prose, tool-call descriptions and tool output stripped, while a separate server-side probe warns the agent when tool output looks like prompt injection.
why: Stripping assistant prose removes its rationalizations and stripping tool results protects the classifier from injection through those results, at the cost of provenance for values such as job IDs.
check: Check whether auto mode can see the authorization or provenance a workflow expects it to use when those details appear only in assistant prose or tool output.
quote: The classifier sees only user messages and the agent's tool calls; we strip out Claude's own messages and tool outputs, making it reasoning-blind by design.

claim: Auto mode's classifier instructions tell it to evaluate an action's real-world impact from the transcript, including a payload Claude writes to a file and then runs, an entire && chain as one action, or a shell command assembled by a Python script.
why: The evaluation rules are designed to account for the effects of an operation even when its wrapper appears benign.
check: When reviewing a classifier verdict on a wrapped command, check the operation the transcript shows it will perform.
quote: The principle is to evaluate the real-world impact of an action, rather than just the surface text of the invocation. The agent shouldn't be able to hide a dangerous operation behind a benign-looking wrapper.

claim: Auto mode runs the classifier at both ends of a subagent handoff: at delegation it can deny, and at return it only prepends a warning to the orchestrator rather than discarding results.
why: Inside a subagent the orchestrator's instruction is the user message, so the outbound check evaluates delegation while the original user's intent is still visible.
check: For auto-mode subagents, check whether the workflow expects a flagged return to be withheld when the classifier only prepends a warning.
quote: Before results go back to the orchestrator, the classifier reviews the subagent's full action history. If it flags, we prepend a security warning for the agent that started the subagent rather than discard the results.

claim: After 3 consecutive classifier denials or 20 in total auto mode stops the model and escalates to the human, and in headless mode (claude -p), where no one can be asked, it terminates the process.
why: This is the backstop against an agent repeatedly pushing towards an outcome the user would not want.
check: For an unattended claude -p job in auto mode, check that the runner handles early termination after repeated classifier denials.
quote: If a session accumulates 3 consecutive denials or 20 total, we stop the model and escalate to the human. This is the backstop against a compromised or overeager agent repeatedly pushing towards an outcome the user wouldn't want. In headless mode (claude -p) there is no UI to ask the human, so we instead terminate the process.

claim: When customizing auto mode, Anthropic recommends editing the shipped baseline shown by claude auto-mode defaults, whose more than twenty block rules are grouped under destroy or exfiltrate, degrade security posture, cross trust boundaries, and bypass review or affect others.
why: The fixed template does the interpretive work and the slots only define policy.
check: For custom auto mode rules, compare the configuration with `claude auto-mode defaults` and check whether the customization builds on the shipped baseline.
quote: If you customize these, we recommend editing this baseline, rather than starting from scratch.

claim: A channel is an MCP server that pushes events into a running session, and being listed in .mcp.json is not enough: the server must also be named in --channels for the session; events only arrive while the session is open.
why: Opting in with --channels is separate from configuring the same server as an ordinary MCP server.
check: Check how sessions are launched (alias, script, service) for --channels entries and whether they are meant to be always-on.
quote: Being in `.mcp.json` isn't enough to push messages: a server also has to be named in `--channels`.

claim: Anyone who can reply through a channel that declares permission relay can approve or deny tool use in the session, so only senders trusted with that authority belong on the channel allowlist.
why: The sender allowlist also gates permission relay.
check: Review the sender allowlist of each channel with permission relay and flag senders who are not trusted to approve or deny tool use.
quote: Anyone who can reply through the channel can approve or deny tool use in your session, so only allowlist senders you trust with that authority.

claim: An interactive channel session pauses for permission prompts until you respond, with permission relay available for remote approval or denial and --dangerously-skip-permissions able to bypass most prompts in trusted unattended environments, subject to actions no mode auto-approves.
why: A channel server can forward permission prompts when it declares the permission relay capability.
check: For a channel using --dangerously-skip-permissions, verify that the environment is trusted and account for actions that still require approval.
quote: For unattended use, [`--dangerously-skip-permissions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode) bypasses most prompts, but only use it in environments you trust. Even then, the [actions no mode auto-approves](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#actions-no-mode-auto-approves) still apply.

claim: For managed channel availability, channelsEnabled is the master switch and defaults to blocked on claude.ai Team and Enterprise, while allowedChannelPlugins replaces the Anthropic allowlist and an empty list still permits the development flag for local testing when channels are enabled.
why: Channel availability depends on the authentication type and the managed settings.
check: If the organization intends to block all channels, verify that channelsEnabled blocks delivery, including for development channels.
quote: If you set an empty array, you block all channel plugins from the allowlist, but `--dangerously-load-development-channels` can still bypass that block for local testing.

claim: During the channels research preview, both --channels and --dangerously-load-development-channels work even though claude --help omits them.
why: The flag syntax and protocol contract may change during the preview.
check: Check startup notices and the effective allowlist if --channels fails to register a plugin, since omission from claude --help does not establish that the flags are unsupported.
quote: Neither `--channels` nor `--dangerously-load-development-channels` appears in `claude --help` while the feature is in preview. The flags work even though they aren't listed.

claim: A mod is a plugin whose JavaScript or TypeScript event handlers run inside the Claude Code process, unlike settings hooks, which are shell commands, HTTP requests or prompts; the docs call both hooks, with settings hook for the settings-file kind.
why: A mod handler can watch, change or take over an event, and can draw interface, which a settings hook cannot.
check: Inspect the modules field in a plugin's hooks/hooks.json for mod entry points and review those modules separately from the settings hooks in the same file.
quote: A mod's handlers are functions that run inside Claude Code instead. Claude Code calls both kinds hooks: on these pages, "hook" means a mod's handler, and the settings-file kind is a "settings hook".

claim: A loaded Claude Code mod runs with the user's access to files and secrets, and processes it starts run outside Claude Code's Bash sandbox.
why: A loaded mod runs inside Claude Code with the user's permissions and can also act on the user's session and spend their model usage.
check: Review the mod's source and claude plugin validate output for file, environment and settings access, prompt or tool-call observation and rewrites, prompt submission as the user, tool approvals and model calls.
quote: Mods aren't sandboxed. If you turn on [sandboxing](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md), the sandbox isolates the Bash commands Claude runs, and a process that a mod starts runs outside it.

claim: A mod can approve many tool calls that the user's deny or ask rules or PreToolUse hooks would stop, while the built-in cc-plugin-sec-default guard prevents a user's mod from doing so by default where it loads.
why: The loaded guard preserves those outcomes by default when a user's mod approves Claude's call.
check: In a local terminal setup that depends on deny rules, ask rules or PreToolUse hooks, check for mods with tool.check and check the Installed tab of /plugin for cc-plugin-sec-default.
quote: With the guard loaded, by default a user's mod can't do this.

claim: claude plugin validate <dir> lists a mod's events on a hooks: line and the mods API methods it calls on a calls: line (for example $.fs.read, $.http.fetch), without running it, so a mod can be reviewed before it is installed.
why: Hooks must use the mods API to reach files, processes and the network, so validate can report the API methods they call without running them.
check: Ask for the validate output of any mod in the setup and look for $.fs.*, $.process.*, $.http.fetch, $.env.*, $.mcp.call and tool.check.
quote: The `hooks:` and `calls:` lines in the output list the events the mod handles and what it asks Claude Code to do.

claim: In ~/.claude/settings.json, disableAllHooks set to true stops user-installed mods, the user's settings hooks and custom status line while organization-managed components keep running.
why: The user setting applies across that user's sessions.
check: Check the user setting when the goal is to stop user-installed mods and account for the hooks and status line it also stops.
quote: Every mod you installed, in every session**: set [`"disableAllHooks": true`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#disableallhooks) in `~/.claude/settings.json`. Your settings hooks and custom status line stop too. What your organization manages keeps running.

claim: Claude Code ships built-in mods listed under Built-in in /plugin, among them cc-plugin-agents-md, which loads AGENTS.md as project instructions in every session that can read it, and cc-plugin-telemetry; disableAllHooks, --bare and --safe-mode do not stop built-in mods.
why: Some of Claude Code's own features are implemented as mods with their own switches.
check: If a setup relies on AGENTS.md, check that the session can read it, cc-plugin-agents-md is enabled and the instruction-file selection permits it.
quote: The settings and flags that stop installed mods, such as `disableAllHooks`, `--bare`, and `--safe-mode`, don't stop built-in mods.

claim: Mod hooks run in claude -p and the Agent SDK, with nothing drawn, but not in a Desktop WSL session, and not in a Desktop SSH session for a mod installed only locally.
why: Plugins are not available in WSL sessions and Desktop does not copy its hooks to the remote machine.
check: If a mod enforces policy, verify it runs on the surfaces in use, including whether the mod is installed on the remote machine for a Desktop SSH session.
quote: No, because plugins aren't available in WSL sessions

claim: By default the built-in guard sec-default@builtin, shown as cc-plugin-sec-default, loads ahead of user-installed mods when the machine has managed settings or managed-mcp.json or the session uses Team or Enterprise /login credentials, and CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN does not count as that login.
why: The guard protects what an organization manages, so it is only loaded where something is managed.
check: Check the machine's managed settings and managed-mcp.json, the session's credential and the guard's presence in /plugin or the debug log before assuming user-installed mods are subject to it.
quote:
The machine has managed settings or a [`managed-mcp.json`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#deploy-managed-mcp-json) file
  * The session runs on [`/login` credentials](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication#authentication-precedence) for a Team or Enterprise plan

claim: Even with the guard loaded, a mod's own $.fs and $.process calls can skip permission rules and PreToolUse hooks (a mod can read .env even with Read(.env) denied), and its $.tool.call and $.mcp.call can skip permission rules, prompts, a hook's ask and the auto mode classifier.
why: A mod's own calls can skip checks that apply to Claude's tool calls, even where the built-in guard is loaded.
check: Check whether a setup relies on Claude's deny rules to protect secrets from a mod's own calls and whether untrusted mods are kept from loading or covered by a policy mod.
quote: With `Read(.env)` denied, a mod can still read that file with `$.fs.read` or start a program that does.

claim: Managed PreToolUse hooks run before any mod's tool.call hook and again on a rewritten call that proceeds, while PreToolUse hooks from other settings files and plugins run after the last mod and are skipped if a mod answers the call itself.
why: Mods are inserted between managed hooks and the other settings hooks.
check: A user or project PreToolUse safety hook is not guaranteed to see a call when an installed mod handles tool.call; check for mods in a setup that relies on such hooks as a guardrail.
quote: A `PreToolUse` hook in managed settings runs before any mod's [`tool.call`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/reference#tools) hook, and when that managed hook blocks a tool call, no mod's `tool.call` hook runs for that call. If the call goes ahead and a mod rewrites it, your managed hooks run again on the rewritten call, so by default they can still block it.

claim: Claude Code reads allowManagedModsOnly only from managed pluginConfigs under cc-plugin-sec-default@builtin, and the built-in guard must load for the option to apply.
why: The guard ignores the same entry in user, project, local and --settings files.
check: Check the exact key in managed settings and confirm that the guard loads when the restriction is supposed to be in effect.
quote: The built-in guard takes options. Set them in managed settings under `pluginConfigs`, keyed by `cc-plugin-sec-default@builtin`, as the example in [Stop user-installed mods from loading](#stop-user-installed-mods-from-loading) does.

claim: In managed settings, disableAllHooks set to true stops every installed plugin's mods and every settings hook, including the organization's own.
why: A managed PreToolUse hook cannot enforce policy while it is off.
check: Flag managed disableAllHooks if the organization relies on a managed PreToolUse hook.
quote: In managed settings, it stops the mods in every installed plugin, yours included, and turns off every hook in settings files, so a `PreToolUse` hook in your managed settings no longer blocks anything.

claim: Managed disableSideloadFlags rejects --plugin-dir, --plugin-url, --agents and --mcp-config at startup and keeps Claude-written mods from loading, while a marketplace allowlist alone still permits loading a mod from any directory with --plugin-dir.
why: A marketplace allowlist restricts marketplace sources but still permits a mod loaded with --plugin-dir unless another control blocks it.
check: If policy requires preventing users from loading mods from arbitrary directories, verify that a control such as disableSideloadFlags blocks that path in addition to the marketplace allowlist.
quote: rejects `--plugin-dir` and `--plugin-url` at startup, and keeps mods Claude writes during a session from loading.

claim: A WebFetch deny rule or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WEB_FETCH leaves mod $.http.fetch available, while an organization policy that disallows WebFetch refuses every mod's fetch request.
why: The WebFetch tool switch and the organization's WebFetch availability policy have different effects on the mods API.
check: Check which WebFetch control is in force before crediting it with blocking mod fetches.
quote: * **You turn off the WebFetch tool with [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_WEB_FETCH`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables) or a `WebFetch` [deny rule](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#tool-specific-permission-rules), in managed settings or any other settings file**: mods can still make `$.http.fetch` requests.

claim: A policy mod's plugin.register hook fails open if it throws or times out without a working .catch refusal, and the policy mod itself can be absent under --safe-mode or after three crashes of the installed-mods worker.
why: Without an error handler the failed hook is skipped, and three worker crashes unload non-built-in mods until /reload-plugins or a new session.
check: Check whether plugin.register has a .catch refusal and whether the workflow accounts for sessions that can run without the policy mod.
quote: If your `plugin.register` hook throws or exceeds its time limit, Claude Code skips the hook, so the check fails open and the mod it was checking loads.

claim: Where the built-in guard loads, only organization-owned mods can use guarded hooks such as prompt.compose, prompt.section, skill.prompt and settings.read.
why: The guard skips user mods' hooks on those events.
check: Check the guarded-event table for classic.<Event>, prompt.compose, prompt.section, prompt.context, prompt.attachment, skill.prompt, attribution.text, session.compact, settings.read and other guarded cases, and look for the skipped-hook note in /plugin on v2.1.299 or later.
quote: Only a plugin that counts as your organization's own runs hooks on these events. An administrator sets that up in managed settings

claim: On v2.1.323 or later a user's mod can keep a managed MCP server from connecting, which /mcp shows as held by that mod, and in an interactive session in an untrusted directory no mod loads until the user answers the trust prompt.
why: Mods can interpose on MCP connection, and the guard does not stop this one.
check: If a managed MCP server is missing in a session, check /mcp for a hold by a mod before blaming the server.
quote: In that user's session, `/mcp` lists the server as held by that mod.

claim: From v2.1.324, a remote-marketplace mod counts as organization-owned when managed settings enable it in enabledPlugins, declare its marketplace in extraKnownMarketplaces and list the plugin ID in prependPlugins or appendPlugins.
why: Organization-owned mods can load where users' mods cannot.
check: Check all required managed entries before treating a remote-marketplace mod as the organization's own.
quote:
To make a mod from a remote marketplace, such as a GitHub repository, count as yours on v2.1.324 or later, do all of these in managed settings:

* Set the mod's plugin to `true` in `enabledPlugins`

claim: A mod's tool.check hook can approve or deny a tool call before the permission prompt, subject to the applicable rules and hooks that take precedence.
why: A tool.check decision can affect what runs and whether the user is asked.
check: Review tool.check in claude plugin validate output and check which permission rules and hooks constrain its decisions.
quote: Can approve or deny a tool call before a permission prompt appears. [Know what happens by default](#know-what-happens-by-default) lists which of your rules and hooks take precedence over its answer.

claim: With the guard loaded, a user's mod cannot rewrite the system prompt, managed CLAUDE.md, the settings-read answer or a connected managed MCP server's tool list or descriptions, and by default it cannot approve Claude's calls past deny rules, ask rules or blocking PreToolUse hooks.
why: With the guard loaded, allowModsToOverrideDenyRules lets a user's mod approve past most outcomes preserved by default, including a deny rule.
check: When relying on the guard to preserve deny rules, verify it loads and check whether managed pluginConfigs sets allowModsToOverrideDenyRules.
quote:
When a user's mod approves Claude's call** with the guard loaded, these outcomes hold [by default](#set-options-on-the-built-in-guard), whichever settings file has the rule or hook:
  * A call that a `deny` rule refuses stays refused
  * A call that an `ask` rule would prompt for still prompts
  * A call that a `PreToolUse` hook blocked stays blocked

claim: A mod's tool.check hook runs after tool.call and PreToolUse and can supply an allow, ask or deny decision subject to permission precedence, while tool.judge runs when auto mode is about to ask its classifier and requires v2.1.326 or later.
why: Calling next in tool.check yields the decision from the rules, permission mode and hooks, and tool.judge can supply a decision at the classifier step.
check: Look for tool.check or tool.judge hooks in a setup that relies on permission or classifier decisions, and verify which decisions the hooks can change.
quote: Claude Code decides whether a tool call may run, after the `tool.call` and `PreToolUse` hooks.

claim: A mod's turn.step hook can change the model or effort for a single request in a Claude Code turn.
why: A turn with tool calls can contain several model requests.
check: Check for turn.step in claude plugin validate if a request uses a model or effort different from the session settings.
quote: `yield* next(e)`, or `next({ ...e, model })`, `next({ ...e, effort })`

claim: From v2.1.321, a mod can invalidate prompt.section or tool.describe and return breakPromptCache set to true to send a changed system prompt section or tool description on the next turn and restart the prompt cache.
why: On versions that require the flag, a section or upfront tool description keeps its saved text without the flag until a new conversation or compaction.
check: Check that a mid-session change invalidates the corresponding hook and sets breakPromptCache, accounting for a slower, more expensive next turn when the cache restarts.
quote: To change a section or a tool description in a running conversation, call `$.ui.invalidate('prompt.section')` or `$.ui.invalidate('tool.describe')` so your hook runs again. Return `{ text, breakPromptCache: true }` or `{ description, breakPromptCache: true }` from it.

claim: A mod's $.prompt.submit with asUser: true sends text as the user's own words, without the sentence that otherwise names the mod as the sender.
why: Without asUser Claude reads submitted text after a sentence that names the mod as its source.
check: Inspect calls to $.prompt.submit for asUser: true when assessing whether a mod can send text presented to Claude as the user's own words.
quote: `submit({ text, asUser: true })` sends the text as the user's own words, without that sentence.

claim: Claude Code skips a mod hook that exceeds its execution limit of 10 seconds per event, or 50 milliseconds for prompt.edit, excluding time in next and API calls other than $.clock.sleep, and a .catch handler has its own 1-second limit.
why: A timeout skips the hook rather than making the hook's intended decision.
check: For a hook meant to refuse an action, check whether it has a .catch handler that refuses on timeout and stays within its own limit.
quote:
A hook's own execution time for one event, not counting time inside `next` or a mods API call other than `$.clock.sleep` | 10 seconds, or 50 milliseconds for a `prompt.edit` hook |
| A `.catch` handler's execution time | 1 second

claim: CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS loads plugin directories like --plugin-dir when set in the environment or in env in ~/.claude/settings.json.
why: The variable provides the equivalent loading path for apps that cannot be passed a flag.
check: Check shell profiles and the user settings env block when an unexpected directory plugin loads.
quote: Environment, or `env` in `~/.claude/settings.json` | Plugin directories to load as `--plugin-dir` does, for apps you can't pass a flag to.

claim: The mod event tool.check fires after the PreToolUse hooks and before the permission prompt, the auto mode classifier and PermissionRequest hooks, so a mod's allow decision there precedes the classifier and the prompt.
why: tool.check is where Claude Code makes the allow, ask or deny decision, and next(e) gives the decision the rules and hooks reached.
check: If a setup relies on auto mode or permission prompts, check what any tool.check hook returns and which rules or hook decisions take precedence over that answer.
quote: after the [`PreToolUse` hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#pretooluse) run, and before the permission prompt,

claim: A mod's tool.call hook can answer a call with a result without calling next, in which case no permission prompt appears, the tool does not run and Claude learns only what the mod returned; it fires for subagent and MCP tool calls too.
why: Returning without next short-circuits the middleware chain, so later mods and Claude Code's own behavior do not run.
check: Transcripts showing a tool result that the tool never produced can point to a mod answering tool.call; check claude plugin validate output for tool.call hooks.
quote: No permission prompt appears and the tool doesn't run, so the result you return is all Claude learns about what happened.

claim: Tool calls the API runs itself, such as the advisor tool, are reported to mods in turn.step's result.serverToolUses from v2.1.290, and no tool.call or tool.check hook fires for them.
why: Claude Code does not run these calls, so the tool-call events never happen.
check: A guardrail built on tool.call or tool.check hooks does not cover server-side tools; do not count it as covering every tool use.
quote: Claude Code doesn't run these calls, so no `tool.call` or `tool.check` hook fires for them.

claim: From v2.1.304, e.isReadOnly in a mod's tool.check hook reflects the tool's own report, and Anthropic advises against approving a call based on that field alone.
why: WebFetch requests a URL and Agent starts a subagent that runs its own tools, though both report as read-only.
check: Check whether a mod relies solely on e.isReadOnly, including reports from Read, Grep, Glob, WebSearch, WebFetch or Agent, Bash's built-in read-only command check, or an MCP server's readOnlyHint set to true.
quote: The value is the tool's own report, so don't approve a call on this field alone.

claim: Hooks on the same event form a chain with the built-in guard where it loads, prependPlugins and other organization-owned mods outside appendPlugins ahead of user-installed mods, then appendPlugins and other built-ins, so each earlier hook sees the event first and can decide whether later hooks run.
why: Hooks on the same event form one middleware chain.
check: When enforcement depends on hook order, verify the loaded mod's tier in the debug log and the configured order in prependPlugins or appendPlugins.
quote: A later mod can't stop an earlier one from seeing an event.

claim: A prompt can go through when a prompt.submit hook throws or times out without a working error handler, when it returns drop after next has let the prompt through, or when the prompt is the command of a skill with context: fork.
why: A failing hook is skipped without a working error handler, and forked-skill commands bypass prompt.submit.
check: Do not treat a prompt.submit mod as a reliable prompt filter; check for a .catch handler and for the forked-skill case.
quote: **The prompt is the `/command` for a [skill with `context: fork`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#run-skills-in-a-subagent)**: your hook doesn't run.

claim: A mod's $.model.complete and $.model.fork bill to the session's plan, API key or cloud provider, with fork sending the conversation and project context as in its last request plus the mod's prompt, and complete sending the mod's prompt as the sole user message without project context.
why: The mods API lets a mod make its own model requests for classifying or summarizing.
check: If usage is higher than the visible conversation explains, check installed mods for model.complete or model.fork in the calls: line of claude plugin validate.
quote: Both calls use the session's credentials, so they bill to the user's plan, API key, or cloud provider.

claim: A mod can register a tool named mcp__<plugin>__<name>, and when MCP tool search defers it, Claude sees the name but not the description until it searches for the tool, unless registration sets isDeferred: false on v2.1.293 or later.
why: Mod-registered tools join Claude's tool list and are handled by tool.call hooks rather than a server.
check: Verify a suspected mod tool's origin through $.tool.register and its matching tool.call hook, then check whether its description is loaded upfront or deferred by MCP tool search.
quote: When [MCP tool search](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#scale-with-mcp-tool-search) defers a registered tool, Claude sees its name but not its description until it searches for it.

claim: A mod that keeps submitting a prompt after every turn can keep a claude -p run alive until stopped unless --max-turns or --max-budget-usd ends it, with mod prompts refused at the limit from v2.1.299 and the mod's subagents counted toward --max-turns from v2.1.304.
why: Each submitted prompt starts another turn.
check: For a headless job with a mod that submits more prompts after each turn, check that the mod stops submitting when done or that the run has a turn or budget limit.
quote: The mod's prompts are refused at the limit from v2.1.299. If your mod spawns subagents, their turns count toward `--max-turns` from v2.1.304.

claim: A Claude Code mod's background timer runs between turns outside any event and can submit a prompt with $.prompt.submit to start a turn once the session is idle.
why: The timer itself starts no turn, and a submitted prompt waits until the session is idle.
check: Check for $.clock.every or $.clock.after and $.prompt.submit if turns start while the user is idle.
quote: When a background job finds something that needs Claude's attention, it can start a turn by submitting a prompt with `$.prompt.submit({ text })`.

claim: In auto and bypassPermissions, Claude Code can enable hot reloading and load a mod it wrote at the end of the turn without asking.
why: Hot reloading runs the session's mods and picks up later changes.
check: Check permission mode and managed loading restrictions when a Claude-written mod appears without a separate approval prompt.
quote: Claude Code can enable hot reloading without asking in `auto` and `bypassPermissions` modes, and the mods load when the turn ends.

claim: A Claude-written mod cannot load in dontAsk or in the claude -p run that writes it in default or acceptEdits.
why: The modes that require approval to hot reload cannot get it in the stated headless case.
check: Distinguish the writing run from a resume and check other loading blockers such as an untrusted interactive workspace, --safe-mode, --bare, disableAllHooks or managed restrictions.
quote: **Nobody is there to approve**: the session is in [`dontAsk` mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes), or it's the `claude -p` run that writes the mod, in `default` or `acceptEdits` mode, which can't show you the hot reloading question.

claim: claude plugin validate also prints env reads/env writes lines and one gating hook without .catch line for each refusing hook lacking an error handler, but it does not catch every event typo: tool.calls fails while tol.call passes validation and the mod then does not load.
why: Validation checks the manifest and statically analyzes the hooks module, so compare registered event names with the types for the build.
check: For hooks expected to refuse an action when their check fails, inspect any gating hook without .catch notice and compare registered event names with the generated types.
quote: Check each event name against [the types for your build](#get-the-types-for-your-build), because validation doesn't catch every typo. For example, `tool.calls` fails with `"tool.calls" is not an event`, but `tol.call` passes validation and the mod then doesn't load.

claim: A plugin checked into a project's .claude/skills/ reaches anyone who clones it and loads only after workspace trust for that folder.
why: The plugin comes from the repository, and trusting a parent folder or using -p alone does not satisfy the trust check.
check: Check whether the session's working directory exposes the checked-in plugin and whether the user accepted workspace trust there.
quote: A project-scope plugin is checked into the repository and reaches every collaborator who clones it. Because that content comes from the repository rather than from you, it loads only after the same trust check that applies to project allow rules in `.claude/settings.json`. Trusting a parent folder or running with `-p` isn't enough.

claim: For each enabledPlugins id, Claude Code uses the highest-priority settings source that mentions it, in descending order from managed to --settings, local, project, user and --add-dir.
why: A source that omits the id leaves the value from a lower-precedence source in effect.
check: Look for a higher-precedence true if a user-disabled plugin loads, check local settings if the user opted out of a project-enabled plugin, and treat managed true or false as final.
quote: For each plugin id, the value that applies is the one from the highest-precedence source that mentions the id.

claim: Plugin auto-update defaults to on for official Anthropic marketplaces and marketplaces added from claude.ai, except knowledge-work-plugins and first-party-plugins, and off elsewhere.
why: A marketplace's explicit autoUpdate setting takes precedence over its default.
check: Check autoUpdate in extraKnownMarketplaces or the /plugin marketplace toggle, and check for headersHelper on any plugin the pass skips.
quote: on for Anthropic's official marketplaces such as `claude-plugins-official`, off for `knowledge-work-plugins` and `first-party-plugins`, on for [marketplaces added from claude.ai](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/install.md#add-from-claude-ai), and off for every other marketplace

claim: For a cached Claude Code plugin whose version comes from its manifest, pinning that string keeps users on the cached copy until the string changes.
why: Claude Code compares computed versions to detect updates, so new commits alone do not replace this cached copy.
check: If an update leaves the cached copy unchanged, check whether the manifest version stayed fixed and whether it determines the computed version for this source.
quote: Because the manifest comes first, a manifest that pins `"version": "1.0.0"` keeps every user on the cached copy until its author changes the string, however many commits they push.

claim: An enabled --plugin-dir, --plugin-url or CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS plugin silently replaces a same-named installed marketplace plugin unless managed enabledPlugins locks the manifest name.
why: A managed entry locks the name whether its value is true or false.
check: Check the debug log for a session-plugin override if the enabled marketplace row appears to point to the wrong copy.
quote:
An enabled `--plugin-dir`, `--plugin-url`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS` plugin. It replaces a same-named installed marketplace plugin or skills-directory plugin:
   * **An installed marketplace plugin**: replaced silently. `claude plugin list` still shows the marketplace row as enabled, because that row reflects your settings.

claim: When caching a plugin with package.json and a supported lockfile at its root, Claude Code attempts to install exact registry dependencies using the npm or Bun selected by that lockfile.
why: The automatic install skips unsupported lockfiles, including yarn.lock and pnpm-lock.yaml, and plugins with dependencies such as git sources.
check: Check the root files and selected package manager, and verify how any unsupported dependencies are installed if the plugin requires them.
quote:
The install runs only when the plugin's root directory contains both a `package.json` and a supported lockfile.

The lockfile decides which package manager Claude Code runs:

claim: Where terminal sync is available, claude.ai plugins, including ones enabled by the organization, load as <name>@synced with their skills, agents, hooks, MCP and LSP servers and the trust of an installed marketplace plugin.
why: Eligible terminal sessions signed into claude.ai sync once in the background at each start from v2.1.273.
check: Use claude plugin list to identify @synced plugins and review their skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers and LSP servers even if the user never installed them locally.
quote:
Each of these plugins loads as `<name>@synced`, with no marketplace and no [install record](#check-which-stage-a-plugin-reached).

In terminal sessions, a synced plugin's skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP servers all load, with the same trust as a marketplace plugin you installed.

claim: A command-sourced plugin reruns its accepted command on install or update and, if enabled, once per session in the background independent of marketplace auto-update, with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC skipping background runs while explicit installs and updates still run it.
why: The printed directory reflects the tool's state when the command ran, so Claude Code refreshes it.
check: Check the accepted marketplace command and whether an enabled command-sourced plugin reruns it shortly after session start even with marketplace auto-update off.
quote: Claude Code skips the two background runs when you set [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars). Explicit installs and updates still run the command with that variable set.

claim: Anthropic's sample Blast Radius mod gates risky Bash commands by inspecting command text, and Anthropic recommends permission rules when a hard block is required.
why: A command-text check cannot account for what indirect commands ultimately execute.
check: Check for a matching permission rule if a setup relies on the Blast Radius confirmation pane for a hard block.
quote: It's a safety net, not a permission system. It reads the command text, so $(…), aliases and scripts that call rm get past it. Use permission rules for a hard block.

claim: The Claude Code mods blog describes a JavaScript environment without DOM or Node access, while the docs say a loaded mod's $ API has the user's access to files, processes and the network.
why: The blog's sandbox refers to the module runtime, while the docs' sandbox refers to the permissions of the loaded mod.
check: Review a mod's calls line for file, process and network operations exposed through the mods API.
quote: The module runs in a sandbox of its own, with no DOM and no Node, so everything outside it goes through $.

claim: Setting autoMode.classifyAllShell to true suspends Bash and PowerShell allow rules in auto mode.
why: Commands that only an allow rule would have approved now wait for a classifier decision.
check: Check autoMode.classifyAllShell if the setup expects narrow shell allow rules to keep working in auto mode.
quote: Set `autoMode.classifyAllShell` to `true` to suspend your Bash and PowerShell allow rules while auto mode is active

claim: Anthropic measured a 0.4% false-positive rate for the full auto mode pipeline on 10,000 tool calls from its employees.
why: Anthropic used actual employee traffic to estimate how often auto mode blocks benign actions.
check: When comparing auto mode with manual approvals, check that estimates of unnecessary blocks are attributed to the internal traffic sample.
quote: Classifier performance by stage. Stage 2 runs only on actions stage 1 flags, so the second row reflects the deployed pipeline end to end: FPR drops from 8.5% to 0.4%, at the cost of some recall.

claim: Anthropic measured a 5.7% false-negative rate for the full auto mode pipeline on 1,000 synthetic data exfiltration attempts.
why: The synthetic dataset measures recall on generated data exfiltration attempts.
check: Check whether any audit finding presents this rate as an estimate from real traffic.
quote:
Synthetic exfil
n=1,000

Stage 1 (fast filter)

8.5% FPR

6.6% FNR

1.8% FNR

Stage 1->Stage 2 (full pipeline)

0.4% FPR

17% FNR

5.7% FNR

claim: Anthropic advises against using auto mode as a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.
why: The classifier sometimes mistakes consent for a related action for consent to the high-stakes action itself.
check: Check whether auto mode has replaced careful human review for high-stakes infrastructure changes.
quote: Auto mode is meant for the first group, and for tasks where the second group's approval overhead isn't worth the marginal safety. It is not a drop-in replacement for careful human review on high-stakes infrastructure.

claim: In the research preview, Claude Code channels require claude.ai authentication or a Console API key and are unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry.
why: Channels depend on Anthropic authentication during the preview.
check: Flag a channels setup that uses an unsupported provider or lacks the required authentication, and check organization enablement separately where required.
quote: > Channels are in [research preview](#research-preview). They require Anthropic authentication through claude.ai or a Console API key, and are not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry. Team and Enterprise organizations must [explicitly enable them](#enterprise-controls).

claim: Mods are on by default in Claude Code, with support from v2.1.287 in the terminal and v2.1.286 in Desktop.
why: Desktop includes its own copy of Claude Code.
check: Check claude --version in the terminal or the Claude Code row in Desktop's /status when assessing mod availability.
quote: Mods are on by default. In the terminal, use Claude Code v2.1.287 or later. The Desktop app includes its own copy of Claude Code, and mods work there from v2.1.286. Check the version in the place you use mods:

claim: Claude Code v2.1.287 and later ignores CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, including when it is set to 0.
why: The variable was an early-access switch.
check: Flag shell profiles that still rely on CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=0 to keep mods off.
quote: > If you set `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS` during early access, remove it. Claude Code v2.1.287 and later ignores it, so setting it to `0` doesn't keep mods off.

claim: With allowManagedModsOnly enabled and the built-in guard loaded, only organization-owned and built-in mods can run their hooks.
why: The option leaves users' settings hooks, status lines and /goal working.
check: Check that user-enabled, --plugin-dir and session-written mods are refused, and confirm the allowManagedModsOnly refusal in the transcript or debug log where sideload flags are available.
quote: | `allowManagedModsOnly` | Users' own mods run | Only [your organization's mods](#install-your-organizations-mods), and mods built into Claude Code, run their hooks. Claude Code refuses every other mod, including one a user installed or named with `--plugin-dir`. |

claim: Managed allowManagedHooksOnly limits mods to the organization's own and Claude Code's built-ins and blocks hooks in users' own settings files.
why: Organizational mods and managed settings hooks remain available under this restriction.
check: Check whether the setup expects user-installed mods or personal settings hooks to run while allowManagedHooksOnly is enabled.
quote: Only [your organization's mods](#install-your-organizations-mods) and the mods built into Claude Code load. A mod a user installed themselves doesn't. The setting also blocks hooks in users' own settings files.

claim: From v2.1.288, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC stops only built-in mods' $.http.fetch requests and requests carrying the session's Anthropic credentials.
why: Before v2.1.288, the variable stopped every mod's $.http.fetch request.
check: Check the version and whether the setup expects this variable to block ordinary fetches from installed mods.
quote: The variable stops only the [mods built into Claude Code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview.md#mods-built-into-claude-code), plus any `$.http.fetch` request that carries the session's Anthropic credentials. Before v2.1.288, the variable stopped every mod's `$.http.fetch` request.

claim: WebFetch controls and CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC do not restrict network access for programs started by a mod through $.process.run.
why: The program runs with the user's network access.
check: Check for $.process.run when assessing whether WebFetch or nonessential-traffic settings cover a mod's network activity.
quote: None of these covers a program the mod starts with `$.process.run`, which reaches the network with the user's own access.

claim: A local-directory mod counts as organization-owned when managed settings enable it in enabledPlugins and declare its marketplace by absolute path, and the marketplace lists the plugin by relative path for in-place loading.
why: Enabling a mod in managed settings alone can still leave it classified as a user's mod.
check: Check the two paths and managed enabledPlugins, then use the debug log to diagnose a mod that still counts as a user's.
quote:
Managed `enabledPlugins` sets the mod's plugin to `true`
* Managed settings name the plugin's [marketplace](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/create-marketplace.md) as a directory on the user's machine, by absolute path. An `extraKnownMarketplaces` entry does that and registers the marketplace for the user too.
* The marketplace lists the plugin by a relative path

claim: When managed prependPlugins is set, the built-in guard loads only if that list includes sec-default@builtin.
why: An explicit prependPlugins list controls whether the guard loads.
check: Check every managed prependPlugins list for sec-default@builtin if the setup relies on the guard.
quote: With `prependPlugins`, also list `sec-default@builtin` to keep the built-in guard.

claim: A mod's session.append hook can rewrite transcript rows such as tool results before storage, except guarded rows and rows holding a skill from an MCP server.
why: The transcript can contain text changed by the mod before it was stored.
check: Check for session.append and any row filters in claude plugin validate when transcript fidelity matters.
quote: Can rewrite each row of the conversation before it's stored, except [the rows the guard passes over](#hooks-the-guard-passes-over) and rows that hold a [skill from an MCP server](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md#use-skills-from-mcp-servers)

claim: A mod's skill.prompt hook can change a skill's text before Claude reads it, including text from an MCP server, subject to the built-in guard.
why: An expanded skill can differ from the skill text on disk or from the MCP server.
check: Check for skill.prompt in claude plugin validate and whether the mod is allowed to run that hook.
quote: Can change a skill's text before Claude reads it, including a skill from an MCP server

claim: A mod's $.env.set changes an environment variable for Claude Code and for commands and MCP servers it starts afterward.
why: The new value can change what those programs run.
check: Review the env writes line from claude plugin validate for variables that affect later commands or MCP servers.
quote: | `$.env.set` | Sets an environment variable for Claude Code and for commands and MCP servers it starts afterward, which can change what those programs run. An `env writes:` line names each variable. |

claim: A mod's prompt.submit hook can rewrite or drop a prompt when it is submitted.
why: Claude can receive different text from the submitted prompt or never receive the prompt at all.
check: Check for prompt.submit if submitted text changes or fails to start a turn.
quote: | [`prompt.submit`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/events#rewrite-or-add-to-a-prompt) | A prompt is submitted | `next({ ...e, text })`, `next({ ...e, context })`, or `{ drop: reason }` |

claim: A mod's prompt.section hook can rewrite or omit a named section of Claude Code's system prompt, subject to the built-in guard.
why: The system prompt sent to Claude can differ from the one Claude Code assembled.
check: Check for prompt.section and whether the mod is allowed to handle it when investigating changed system instructions.
quote: Once for each named section of the system prompt. `e.name` is the section's `id` in `prompt.compose`. | `{ text }`, or `{ text: null }` to omit the section.

claim: A mod's prompt.attachment hook can rewrite or omit a message Claude Code adds for Claude, such as a reminder, subject to the built-in guard.
why: The message Claude reads can differ from the one Claude Code generated.
check: Check for prompt.attachment and whether the mod is allowed to handle it when a built-in reminder is changed or missing.
quote: | `prompt.attachment` | Claude Code adds a message of its own for Claude, such as a reminder. `e.type` names the kind, and for the kinds the types declare, `e.detail` holds the facts the text was written from. | `{ text }`, or `{ text: null }` to omit it |

claim: A mod's prompt.context hook can change the context sent with a conversation's first message, subject to the built-in guard.
why: The first request can receive context blocks supplied by the mod.
check: Check for prompt.context when first-message context differs from expectations, and check skill.prompt separately if the discrepancy is in expanded skill text.
quote: | [`prompt.context`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/events#rewrite-or-add-to-a-prompt) | Once for each conversation, for the context sent with the first message | `{ blocks }` |

claim: A mod's agent.spawn hook can choose the model of a subagent that is starting.
why: A subagent's request can use a model different from the one configured for it.
check: Check for agent.spawn if a newly started subagent runs on an unexpected model.
quote: A subagent or an [agent team](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams.md) teammate is about to start, or a subagent that finished or stopped is about to run again. For a teammate, `e.isTeammate` is `true`. For a resumed run, `e.resume` is set. | `next({ ...e, model })` to choose the model of one that is starting, or `{ deny: reason }`

claim: From Claude Code v2.1.328, a mod's tool.offer hook can withhold a tool from Claude.
why: Claude Code consults this hook when it builds the tool list and again when Claude calls a tool.
check: Check for tool.offer if a tool is missing and whether the built-in guard protects the tool list at issue.
quote: Claude Code builds Claude's tool list, and again when Claude calls a tool. Requires Claude Code v2.1.328 or later. | `next(e)`, or `{ isOffered: false }` to withhold the tool from Claude.

claim: A mod's agent.offer hook can withhold a subagent type from Claude.
why: A configured subagent can be absent from the choices offered to Claude.
check: Check for agent.offer if Claude is missing a subagent type that the setup defines.
quote: | `agent.offer` | A subagent type is offered to Claude | `{ isOffered: false }` to withhold it |

claim: From v2.1.331, a mod can invalidate tool.offer and return breakPromptCache set to true to update the main conversation's tool list and restart the prompt cache.
why: The update discards the cached prompt prefix for the conversation.
check: Check how often a mod invalidates tool.offer and restarts the cache when changing tool availability mid-session.
quote: To change the main conversation's tool list, call `$.ui.invalidate('tool.offer')` and return `{ isOffered, breakPromptCache: true }` from your `tool.offer` hook. The [prompt cache](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/prompt-caching.md) then starts over. Requires Claude Code v2.1.331 or later.

claim: Claude Code honors prependPlugins and appendPlugins in user settings only if the machine has neither managed settings nor managed-mcp.json and the session uses no Team or Enterprise /login credential.
why: Managed settings are the normal source for these plugin ordering lists in managed setups.
check: Check the machine's managed files and the session's credential before relying on either user setting.
quote: Managed settings. User settings only on a machine with no managed settings or [`managed-mcp.json`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/managed-mcp#deploy-managed-mcp-json) file, in a session whose credential isn't a Team or Enterprise `/login`.

claim: A mod's $.ui.notify uses the user's preferredNotifChannel for terminal notifications, and Claude Code sets no rate limit on those notifications.
why: The mod cannot select the channel.
check: Check preferredNotifChannel and calls to $.ui.notify if a mod sends unexpected or frequent terminal notifications.
quote: A notification from their terminal, outside Claude Code, sent the way their [`preferredNotifChannel`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#preferrednotifchannel) setting says.

claim: When a mod's $.ui.notify reaches a running session, the user's Notification hooks run with type plugin_notification even if terminal delivery is disabled or unavailable.
why: The hook that made the notification call is excluded from that run.
check: Check Notification matchers for plugin_notification when a mod notification triggers a hook despite no terminal delivery.
quote: When the call reaches a running session, the user's [`Notification` hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#notification) run with the type `plugin_notification`. They run even when the answer is `disabled`, and in a session with no terminal, where the answer is `no-surface`.

claim: In a new interactive session in default or acceptEdits, Claude Code prompts for each Claude-written mod file and, if mods can load, asks about hot reloading on the first save.
why: The mods folder is protected, and hot-reload approval lasts for that session and its resumes.
check: Check the file-approval and first-save hot-reload prompts when reviewing authorization for a Claude-written mod.
quote: In the `default` and `acceptEdits` [permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md), Claude Code asks you to approve each of the mod's files before Claude creates it

claim: When an eligible Claude Code session resumes interactively or with claude -p, mods already in its session mods folder can load without asking.
why: Choosing Not now at the first hot-reload prompt leaves the files in place for the next start of that session.
check: Inspect the session's folder under ~/.claude/dev-mods and the loading restrictions if an existing mod appears on resume.
quote: When you resume a session, interactively or with `claude -p`, the mods already in its mods folder [can load](#sessions-that-cant-load) without asking. To keep a mod from loading when you resume, delete its directory.

claim: Claude Code deletes the session's Claude-written mods folder once it is older than cleanupPeriodDays.
why: A Claude-written mod loads only in the session that made it unless it is copied out and loaded separately.
check: Check cleanupPeriodDays and the session's mods folder when investigating why a previously written mod is gone.
quote: A mod Claude wrote loads only in the session that made it, and Claude Code deletes that session's mods folder once it's older than [`cleanupPeriodDays`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#cleanupperioddays).

claim: MCP servers declared by a plugin in a project's .claude/skills/ go through the same per-server approval as project .mcp.json servers if the declaration is eligible.
why: Claude Code skips bundle declarations and server files outside the plugin directory.
check: Check per-server approval and whether the declaration is inline or in a .mcp.json file inside the plugin directory.
quote: * MCP servers it declares go through the [same per-server approval](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md) as a project `.mcp.json`

claim: Claude Code skips background monitors in plugins shared through a repository, whether listed under `enabledPlugins` in `.claude/settings.json` or placed under the project's `.claude/skills/`.
why: The repository trust check and component limits do not apply to plugins under ~/.claude/skills/.
check: Flag reliance on a background monitor from a project skills-directory plugin.
quote:
* [Background monitors](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/components.md#monitors) do not load

Neither the trust check nor these component limits apply to a plugin under your own `~/.claude/skills/`.

claim: By default, a plugin enabled only in a project's .claude/settings.json needs a local install before Claude Code loads it at session start.
why: Project enablement alone does not usually place the plugin on disk.
check: Check the installed copy and /plugin Errors, and account for install-free seed directories or relative-path entries in local-path or git marketplaces.
quote: By default, a plugin enabled only in your project's `.claude/settings.json` doesn't load at session start until you install it on your machine.

claim: DISABLE_UPDATES=1, DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1 turns off Claude Code's plugin auto-update pass unless FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1 is also set.
why: With the pass off, Claude Code also hides the marketplace auto-update toggle.
check: Check these environment variables if plugin auto-update does not run or the toggle is missing.
quote: If you set `DISABLE_UPDATES=1`, `DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1`, or `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1`, the whole pass is off and the auto-update toggle is hidden, unless you also set `FORCE_AUTOUPDATE_PLUGINS=1`.

claim: For github, url and git-subdir plugins with no version in the manifest or marketplace entry, Claude Code uses a 12-character commit SHA and adds a path hash for git-subdir.
why: For these sources, the manifest version takes precedence over the marketplace version, and both take precedence over a value from the commit.
check: Check both version fields and the source commit or subdirectory when auditing a Git-based plugin's cached version.
quote:
3. When neither is set, the version comes from the source type:

| Source type | Version when no `version` field is set |
| :- | :- |
| `github`, `url`, or `git-subdir` | The commit SHA of the source, shortened to 12 characters. A `git-subdir` version also carries a hash of the subdirectory path |

claim: With no version in the manifest or marketplace entry, Claude Code uses unknown for npm plugins and for local directory plugins whose directory and marketplace are not Git repositories.
why: The fallback depends on the source type.
check: If an npm or directory plugin reports unknown, check the manifest and entry for a version and whether the directory or marketplace is a git repository.
quote:
| Local directory, when neither the plugin directory nor its marketplace is a git repository | `unknown` |
| `npm` | `unknown` |

claim: When two enabled plugins from different marketplaces share a manifest name, both can show as enabled in /plugin while only one copy's hooks run.
why: The managed-enabled copy holds the name if there is one, otherwise the first copy Claude Code loads holds it.
check: Check /plugin Errors for the copy whose hooks were left out, using v2.1.296 or later for the note.
quote: When you install and enable two plugins with the same manifest name from different marketplaces, both appear as enabled in `/plugin`, but the hooks of one of them are left out. One plugin per name registers the hooks in its `hooks/hooks.json`, and one plugin per name loads a [hooks module](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/plugins/mods/overview.md).

claim: Claude Code disables lifecycle scripts during automatic plugin dependency installation.
why: Packages that build native modules in lifecycle scripts can download without compiling during the automatic install.
check: Check whether a missing native module needs an install step that runs its lifecycle scripts.
quote: * **No lifecycle scripts**: `--ignore-scripts` keeps `preinstall`, `install`, and `postinstall` scripts from running, so dependencies that build native modules in those scripts download but don't compile during this install

claim: Claude Code treats an automatic plugin dependency install that exceeds 60 seconds as failed.
why: Claude Code limits how long a dependency install can run.
check: Check for a timeout if an automatic install leaves the plugin without its dependencies.
quote: * **60-second timeout**: Claude Code stops an install that runs longer and treats it as failed

claim: Claude Code provides no setting or environment variable to turn off automatic plugin dependency installation.
why: The install is part of caching a plugin with eligible dependencies.
check: Flag configurations that rely on a setting or environment variable to skip a plugin's otherwise eligible automatic install.
quote: You can't turn the automatic install off. No setting or environment variable disables it.

claim: A synced plugin an organization marks as required on claude.ai loads even if the user tries to disable that plugin individually.
why: In claude plugin list, the plugin is marked required by your org.
check: Check the required marker when a disabled @synced plugin still loads.
quote: a plugin that your organization marks as required on claude.ai loads even if you disabled it earlier.

claim: Setting syncClaudeAiPlugins to false stops Claude Code from downloading claude.ai plugins and from loading previously synced plugins on the next start.
why: The setting applies machine-wide when set in user or managed settings.
check: Check syncClaudeAiPlugins and restart status if @synced plugins are expected to stop loading.
quote: Claude Code stops downloading, and the next time you start it, it moves the plugins it already synced to `~/.claude/plugins/.trash/` and no longer loads them.
